about: Art direction for the Images studio (from the Python app's (0.16) art_direction.py). 'game-concept' is the recipe the owner called fantastic (2026-10-25): AMAL's prompt + FLUX.2 klein 4B on NVIDIA's free API. The ref-* styles are 3D model references in different art styles (realistic, stylized, toon, hand-painted, chibi, low-poly, voxel, clay) - framed the same way (reference_shot), so the owner can pick a look (2026-11-01). A goal that names one of these (said_as: "low-poly") gets that style only, four takes of it.

for_objects.about: A subject that is an object (a chest, a sword, a house) is drawn as a prop: the style's object_form is used and this is said with it, so it never grows a face or legs (2026-11-05: three of four chest references came back as creatures). Never list body parts here: "no face, no arms, no legs" next to "treasure chest" was refused by FLUX's safety filter on every try (2026-11-05); the technical-artist check asks about faces and limbs instead.
for_objects.add: an object, not a creature or a character

reference_shot.about: How every ref-* picture is framed, in plain sentences after the style (FLUX.2 reads prose, subject and style first; a long tag list was cut and diluted the style, 2026-11-05). Never the word silhouette: FLUX drew four swords as black silhouettes from it.. One shot for all styles so the 3D model maker gets the same view. Rendered as a 3D model, never a flat drawing: TRELLIS.2 learned from rendered 3D objects, and a flat outlined cartoon fox gave it a black texture (2026-11-05).
reference_shot.creature: Shown alone and whole with space around it, standing in a relaxed A-pose with arms and legs clear of the body, every part shown once, in a three-quarter front view at eye level
reference_shot.object: Shown alone and whole with space around it, every part shown once and nothing cut off, in a three-quarter front view at eye level
reference_shot.all: Rendered as a 3D model with real depth and soft shading on every surface, not a flat 2D drawing or line art. Even soft studio light, no cast shadow, a plain flat light grey background, clean readable shapes, every surface lit and in full colour, everything in focus

turn.edit: Turn the {subject} around: show it from directly behind, a straight back view. The exact same character with the same body, proportions, colours, clothing and pose, at the same size and place in the picture - now we see the back of its head and its back, and no face. Keep the plain background and the even light.
turn.check: Is it seen from behind - the back of its head and body towards us, its face not visible?

turn.edit: Turn the {subject} a quarter turn: show it from the side in pure profile, facing the right edge of the picture. The exact same character with the same body, proportions, colours and clothing, standing upright at the same size, arms hanging a little away from the body - we see one side of its head and one arm and leg in front. Keep the plain background and the even light.
turn.check: Is it seen from the side in profile - one side of the head, not the front of the face and not the back?
turn.faces: Which edge of the picture does its nose (the front of its face and its toes) point at?

turn.edit: Turn the {subject} a quarter turn: show it from the side in pure profile, facing the left edge of the picture. The exact same character with the same body, proportions, colours and clothing, standing upright at the same size, arms hanging a little away from the body - we see one side of its head and one arm and leg in front. Keep the plain background and the even light.

reference_shot.turn_about: The views drawn from a front picture by the edit model for a 3D model built from several views (the `views` tool): the edit's words ({subject} is the job's subject), the question a vision model must answer yes to, `turned`: the view's outline must differ from the front's (a side view), `mirror`: the view its mirror image gives, `unless`: a view that makes this one unneeded (the other profile is tried only when the first did not pass). In the maker's `left` view the subject faces the right edge of the picture (Comfy-Org's Pixal3D multi-view template).

compact.about: NVIDIA's hosted FLUX.2 klein reads only about the first 300 characters of a prompt (measured 2026-11-10: the same picture, byte for byte, whatever came after character 317; a change after 280 changed it). Everything said later - the pose, the view, the background, the light, the no-text clause - was never read: references came back three-quarter, crouching, on floors with shadows, and every style looked the same. So a reference is one sentence inside `reads` characters: the view and kind first, the style's `short`, the subject (cut to the room left), the pose and the background. `front` is the straight front view a rig and a model built from several views need; {pose} is one of `poses` (the 3D line's Pose). The long words (form, words, all) follow for models that read further.

compact.object: Three-quarter front view 3D model reference, {style}, of {subject}, shown whole and alone, plain grey background

prompt_expert.about: The Prompt Expert (brought back from the Python app (0.16) prompt_expert.py; owner 2026-10-27: "every prompt should go through a prompt expert ... the current prompts suck", 2026-11-09: "we need better prompt engineers after people prompt"). Every prompt a job writes for a picture is rewritten once by the strongest model as an art director would, before anything is drawn. `system` are its rules; `for_reference` is added when the picture is a reference a 3D model is built from; the style's own finishing words are added afterwards and never repeated. An `image` call with exact: true keeps its prompt word for word.
prompt_expert.system:
You are the Prompt Expert of a small game studio: an art director who rewrites the prompts other agents write for an image model (FLUX class). Make the picture the owner will love.
Rules:
- Plain, vivid, specific English, at most 45 words - the hosted picture model reads only about the first 300 characters, so every word counts and the most important comes first. Subject first: what it is, its build, materials, colours, pose and expression; then composition and camera (framing, angle), light (direction, quality, time of day), palette and mood.
- One clear subject unless the brief needs more. Concrete nouns and adjectives; never vague praise (beautiful, masterpiece, 8k, trending), keyword soup, weights or parentheses.
- No words in the picture, and never name what to avoid as a positive (write "an empty sky", not "no text").
- Keep everything the original asked for (subject, style, view, pose, background, every named thing). Fix what is vague or missing with concrete choices that fit the job.
- The style's finishing words are added afterwards automatically: do not write a style list.
Answer with JSON only: {"prompt": "...", "why": "one short line: what you changed"}
prompt_expert.for_reference: This picture is the reference a 3D model is built from: describe only what the subject IS, in at most 18 words - its build, its main parts, materials and colours, what it wears. Leave out pose, action, mood, camera, background, light and style (the 3D line frames every reference the same way, and the picture model reads only the start of a prompt).
